query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, a friction‐induced, transient oxide film forms on the eutectic HEA but then undergoes mechanical spallation due to mismatched strain and thermal expansion between the alternating phases. Once fragmented, the newly exposed microstructural interfaces, which have different electrochemical potentials, act as localized galvanic cells that accelerate pitting and dissolution. This synergy between mechanical film breakdown and microgalvanic corrosion drives the accelerated overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine lamellar microstructure (e.g., alternating FCC and BCC/B2 phases) that, when exposed to high temperature in an oxidizing environment, forms a thin protective oxide/tribo-layer.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to a controlled reciprocating wear test combined with a corrosive (chloride-rich) environment at elevated temperature. In a controlled comparison, modify a set of samples by adding a minor oxide‐stabilizing element (e.g., trace Y or Hf) aimed at enhancing oxide film adhesion, while leaving a matched baseline alloy unmodified.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (approximately 800–900 °C) under an atmosphere containing oxygen and chloride species (simulating hot corrosion conditions), with cyclic mechanical loading (reciprocating wear) applied to induce frictional heating and stress.
generation.structural_mediator: The interlamellar phase boundaries between the distinct FCC and BCC/B2 phases, which due to their compositional differences have different mechanical and electrochemical properties and facilitate localized galvanic interactions when exposed.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, frictional heating promotes rapid oxidation so that a protective oxide film initially forms on the alloy surface. However, due to the differential thermal expansion and mechanical properties of the alternating phases, cyclic loading creates local stresses that cause the oxide film to spall. This exposes discrete regions of the underlying heterogeneous microstructure that, because of their disparate electrochemical potentials, set up microgalvanic couples. The resulting localized pitting corrosion then synergizes with the mechanical wear, causing an overall degradation rate that is higher than the sum of individual wear or corrosion damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline (or isolated wear/corrosion tests), the alloy under simultaneous wear-corrosion will exhibit a total degradation (increased mass loss, deeper wear tracks, and greater pitting density) significantly higher than expected from additive effects. Conversely, the modified alloy with enhanced oxide adhesion should display lower wear depths and fewer corrosion pits. Specifically, the baseline should show an accelerated degradation due to oxide spallation and microgalvanic attack while the modification mitigates these localized failures.
generation.baseline: The matched baseline is the unmodified eutectic HEA tested under identical high-temperature, chloride-containing, cyclic wear conditions, with separate control tests in only wear or only corrosion environments.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate only when the temperature is high enough (near or above 800 °C) to induce rapid oxidation and significant thermal expansion mismatches, and when the corrosive species (e.g., Cl–) are present to drive microgalvanic corrosion. At lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres, the protective oxide layer remains stable, and the coupled degradation is not observed.
generation.uncertainty: While individual studies (e.g., PMC12156342 showing friction-induced oxide spalling and PMC12735082 along with PMC9319277 demonstrating microgalvanic corrosion in eutectic HEAs) independently suggest these processes, the precise synergy between mechanical film breakdown and galvanic pitting in a multi-phase eutectic structure under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions has not been fully quantified. The current proposal extends these findings to assert that their coupling is the dominant mechanism under the specified extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: (1) a baseline set and (2) a set modified with trace additions (e.g., Y or Hf) to bolster oxide adhesion. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear and chloride-rich corrosion tests at 850 °C using a reciprocating tribometer. For comparison, perform separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests under the same temperature conditions.
measurements: Wear depth and volume loss (via laser scanning microscopy or 3D profilometry)
Corrosion rate and pitting density (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and microscopic analysis)
Surface oxide film integrity and spallation (using high-temperature in-situ microscopy and post-test SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% improvement) in overall degradation, pitting density, and wear depth compared to the baseline under simultaneous tests—or if the degradation observed in simultaneous wear-corrosion tests matches the simple additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion—then the hypothesis that the accelerated degradation is driven by synergistic oxide film spallation coupled with interphase galvanic corrosion is refuted.

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

In this paper, we investigated the influence of post-heat treatment on the microstructure and corrosion property of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA prepared by LMD, and the following conclusions can be obtained: The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, whether heat-treated or not, exhibited typical dual-phase lamellar structure compromising FCC and BCC phases. With the increase in temperature of the heat treatment, the volume fraction of the FCC phase and interlamellar spacing both increased. The phase constitution obtained after heat treatment at 800 °C was the closest to the equilibrium state of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA. As the heating temperature was elevated, the resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to uniform corrosion was gradually enhanced. This was ascribed to the consistent increase in the volume fraction of the FCC phase in the alloy with the increasing heating temperature. The sample heat-treated at 1000 °C exhibited best resistance to uniform corrosion. Potentiodynamic polarization and immersion tests both suggest that the samples heat-treated at 800 and 1000 °C suffered more severe pitting corrosion than the as-prepared and 600 °C-treated samples.
